intro: Each case study below is built from documented campaign exports. Where the evidence supports a conclusion, it is stated plainly. Where it does not, that is stated just as plainly.

summary.cardTitle: Scaling Meta Lead Generation in Patna
summary.subtitle: {{metric:re.cohort_2025.leads}} → {{metric:re.cohort_2026.leads}} leads across observed campaign cohorts, while reported CPL fell {{metric:re.cohort.cpl_change_pct}}.

cta.heading: Running Meta lead campaigns?

sections.heading: What Meta was actually optimising for
What this evidence does not establish

body: The cohorts below are grouped by campaign start year and include only campaigns that recorded results.

This is an observed comparison, not a controlled before/after experiment. Spend levels, projects, creative and platform delivery all changed between the two cohorts, so the difference in cost per lead cannot be attributed to any single decision.

cohortObservations: Reported CPL fell {{metric:re.cohort.cpl_change_pct}} across the observed cohorts.

resultTypesTable.caption: Meta result types and reported cost per result
resultTypesTable.note: Meta quality-lead optimisation is a platform optimisation setting with its own reported cost per result. The {{metric:re.result_type.quality_lead.cost_per_result}} figure is not a measure of independently verified, human-qualified leads and is not described as one anywhere on this site.

content.resultTypesChipNote: The {{metric:re.result_type.quality_lead.cost_per_result}} figure is Meta’s cost per quality-optimised result, not a verified human-qualified lead cost.
resultTypesCommentary: These four result types are not interchangeable. A messaging conversation, a lead form submission, a quality-optimised lead and a native call are different events with different downstream value, so comparing their cost per result only means something once you have decided which event actually matters to the business.
That decision is a business question rather than a platform question — and it is the one worth settling before any of these numbers is used to move budget.
content.campaignsIntro: {{metric:re.top5.campaign_count|words_capitalised}} campaigns account for {{metric:re.top5.leads}} of the recorded leads. The spread between the cheapest and the most expensive is close to {{metric:re.top5.cpl_spread}}, which is the more useful number: it says the difference sits in the campaign, not in the platform.

campaignsTable.caption: {{metric:re.top5.campaign_count|words_capitalised}} campaigns by recorded leads and cost per lead
campaignsTable.note: Blended CPL is combined spend divided by combined recorded leads across these {{metric:re.top5.campaign_count|words}} campaigns only. It is not the account-level figure.

content.variantsIntro: {{metric:re.variant.campaign_count|words_capitalised}} campaigns ran alongside a variant. The exports record what each one spent and produced; they do not record why the variant was created.
content.variantNote: The exports show performance differences between campaign variants, but they do not establish the original decision rationale. Nothing here should be read as a claim that a particular creative or copy change caused a particular outcome.
blendedMethodology: {{metric:re.blended_cpl}} divides all lead-objective spend by Meta form submissions, and it includes {{metric:re.zero_result_lead_spend}} of lead campaigns that recorded no results.

A more flattering figure is available by excluding that spend. It is not used here. Spend that produced no recorded result is still spend, and a cost-per-lead number that quietly removes it is not a number worth planning a budget against.
content.scaleNote: The exports record that Hindi and English creative variants existed. They do not record a language attribute for every creative, so {{metric:re.structure.ads}} is a count of ads, not a count of bilingual creative pairs.
content.limitationsIntro: The available evidence covers platform-recorded activity. It does not confirm any of the following:

takeaway.heading: Scaling lead volume is only half the job.
body: The cohort data shows what a paid social account can do once structure, targeting and creative volume are working: more spend absorbed, considerably more recorded leads, a materially lower reported cost per lead.

It also shows the ceiling of platform-only measurement. Every figure on this page stops at the form submission. The next layer — and the more valuable one — is connecting ad-platform results with lead quality and downstream business outcomes, so that cheaper leads can be tested against better leads rather than assumed to mean the same thing.

summary.title: I Audited My Own Ad Accounts Before Optimising Them
summary.subtitle: {{metric:audit.unreliable_share|percent_0dp}} of the spend was reporting numbers I could not trust.
summary.cardDescription: A review of {{metric:site.accounts|words}} ad accounts across Meta and Google, carried out before treating any performance number as a basis for optimisation.
summary.metaDescription: A measurement audit of {{metric:site.accounts|words}} Meta and Google ad accounts: inflated conversion reporting, placeholder values, unverified conversion actions and incomplete tracking, with the limitations stated.

cta.heading: Not sure whether your conversion data is trustworthy?
cta.body: That is exactly what a free ad audit is for.

sections.heading: Two campaign types, two measurement states
What this review does not establish

heroMetrics.label: associated with unreliable, unverified or inflated measurement

situation: {{metric:site.accounts|words_capitalised}} ad accounts across Meta and Google were reviewed before treating performance numbers as optimisation truth.

The order matters. Optimising against a conversion column you have not checked is not optimisation — it is guessing with extra steps. So before any budget decision, the question was narrower and duller: do these numbers describe something real, and do they describe the same thing consistently?
For roughly a third of the documented spend, the answer was no.
content.situationNote: The exact technical cause of every issue was not established from the exports alone, and none is asserted here.

auditChecks.title: Conversion recording
auditChecks.description: Whether the account records conversions at all, and in which column.

auditChecks.title: Conversion plausibility vs clicks
auditChecks.description: Whether reported conversion counts and rates are arithmetically possible given recorded click volume.

auditChecks.title: Conversion diagnostics
auditChecks.description: The platform’s own status flags on each conversion action.

auditChecks.title: Placeholder values
auditChecks.description: Conversion values that are defaults or stand-ins rather than real business values.

auditChecks.title: Agreement between reports
auditChecks.description: Whether campaign-level and account-level figures reconcile with each other.

auditChecks.title: Measurement parity across campaign types
auditChecks.description: Whether different campaign types in the same account are measured on comparable terms.

auditChecks.title: Conversion-action status
auditChecks.description: Whether each conversion action is verified, active and currently recording.

auditChecks.title: Platform events vs business outcomes
auditChecks.description: Whether a recorded platform event can be tied to a defined business outcome at all.

scaleFlow.label: Spend where measurement did not hold up

failureModes.title: Inflated conversion reporting
failureModes.summary: Reported conversion rates that cannot be reconciled with recorded click volume.
body: One Google account reported campaign-level conversion rates far above 100%, alongside an account-level figure of {{metric:audit.acct_inflated.conv_rate}}.

A conversion rate above 100% is not automatically an error — duplicate counting, multi-conversion actions and attribution settings can all produce one legitimately. What it is, always, is a signal to stop and check before the number is used to justify a budget change.

table.caption: Campaign-level reported conversion rates in the affected account
table.note: Campaigns are numbered rather than named here because the point is the pattern across the account, not any individual campaign.

failureModes.caution: The exports show mathematically implausible conversion reporting; the precise technical cause was not established from the exports alone.

failureModes.title: Placeholder values
failureModes.summary: Conversion values recorded as {{metric:audit.placeholder_conversion_value}} rather than a real business value.
body: {{metric:audit.placeholder_value_campaigns|words_capitalised}} campaigns contained {{metric:audit.placeholder_conversion_value}} conversion values.

A {{metric:audit.placeholder_conversion_value}} value is a placeholder, not a price. Any downstream figure built on it — conversion value, value per conversion, ROAS — inherits the placeholder and reports it as though it were revenue.
failureModes.caution: Value-based reporting was therefore not meaningful for those campaigns, and no value-based metric from them appears anywhere on this site.

failureModes.title: Unverified or inactive conversion actions
failureModes.summary: Conversion actions present in the account but not verified and not currently recording.
body: In one preschool account, the platform’s own diagnostics flagged a set of conversion actions as unverified or dormant, while campaigns in that account continued to spend.

The Performance Max campaign in the same account is the clearest illustration: substantial click volume at a low cost per click, a lead-funnel figure reported in one place, and nothing at all in the conversions column.
failureModes.caution: A campaign recording 0 conversions in the platform’s conversion column is a statement about measurement, not about whether the campaign produced enquiries. This review does not establish that it produced none.

failureModes.title: Incomplete or zero-result tracking
failureModes.summary: Spend running against campaigns with no usable recorded outcome.
body: Across two further preschool accounts and a set of Meta website lead campaigns, spend accumulated against tracking that was incomplete or recorded no results.
This is the least dramatic failure mode and the most common one. Nothing looks broken on the surface; the account simply cannot answer the question it is being asked.

metrics.label: sources: two preschool accounts and Meta website lead campaigns

failureModes.caution: This describes the state of the recorded tracking. It does not establish that these campaigns generated no enquiries, and it does not identify the technical cause.

content.failureModesNote: The three spend figures above — {{metric:audit.acct_inflated.spend}}, {{metric:pre.account_a.spend}} and {{metric:audit.incomplete_tracking.spend}} — sum to the {{metric:audit.unreliable_spend}} quoted at the top of this page.
content.campaignTypesIntro: Two campaign types in the same account, presented side by side because they were measured on completely different terms — not because one of them won.
content.campaignTypesCaution: This is not evidence that Search outperformed PMax. The sample and measurement conditions are not comparable enough to make that conclusion.

lesson.heading: The first optimisation decision was measurement integrity — not scaling.
body: Every action available in an ads platform — raising budgets, pausing campaigns, shifting spend between channels, changing bid strategy — depends on the conversion column being a reasonable description of reality.
Where it is not, optimisation does not merely fail to help. It actively moves budget towards whichever campaign happens to be miscounting most confidently.
So the first piece of work in these accounts was not a scaling decision. It was establishing which numbers had earned the right to be optimised against.

content.limitationsIntro: This review was carried out on exported reporting. It does not establish:
limitations: The precise technical cause of any issue
content.limitationsClosing: This was a review of exported reporting, not a technical tracking audit of the live accounts. A live audit — tag firing, event parameters, conversion action configuration, deduplication — is a separate piece of work and would be needed to establish causes.

summary.metaDescription: Google Ads case study across {{metric:pre.accounts|words}} preschool accounts: Performance Max, Smart and Search campaign performance, conversion diagnostics, and why reported activity and recorded conversions did not line up.

cta.heading: Seeing conversions you can’t confidently explain?
cta.body: That is worth diagnosing before you spend another rupee against them.

sections.heading: Account A — Performance Max at scale, nothing recorded
Account B — spend without recorded outcomes
Account C — the smallest account, the clearest signal
What this diagnosis does not establish

heroMetrics.label: reported lead-funnel leads vs recorded conversions in one campaign

intro: {{metric:pre.accounts|words_capitalised}} preschool accounts, {{metric:pre.accounts|words}} different campaign-type mixes, and one recurring problem: the numbers describing activity and the numbers describing outcomes were not talking to each other.
This page walks each account in turn. It is a diagnosis of what the reporting can and cannot support — not a claim about which campaigns produced admissions.

terminology.definition: A conversion recorded in the platform’s own conversions column.
terminology.note: Every use of “recorded” or “verified conversion” on this page carries the narrow meaning above and nothing more.

accounts.name: {{label:Pinwheel|Preschool account A}}
intro: The largest of the {{metric:pre.accounts|words}} accounts, and the one where the gap between reported activity and recorded outcomes is widest.

The Performance Max campaign absorbed the majority of the spend and produced a large volume of clicks at around a rupee each. In one report it shows {{metric:pre.account_a.pmax.reported_funnel_leads}} lead-funnel leads. In the conversions column it shows nothing.
accounts.note: The two campaigns above are the ones relevant to this diagnosis; together they do not account for the full {{metric:pre.account_a.spend}} of account spend.
accounts.caution: The Search campaign recorded {{metric:pre.account_a.search.clicks}} clicks. That sample is far too small, and the account’s measurement far too unreliable, to support any conclusion about Search performing better than Performance Max here.

accounts.name: {{label:Birla Open Minds|Preschool account B}}
intro: Nearly two thousand recorded clicks across two campaign types, and a single recorded conversion between them.

A Smart campaign spent {{metric:pre.account_b.smart.spend}} for {{metric:pre.account_b.smart.clicks}} clicks and recorded nothing. The Search campaign spent nearly four times as much for fewer clicks and recorded one conversion.
accounts.caution: One recorded conversion is not a performance signal. It is a prompt to check whether the conversion action was configured and firing across both campaign types on the same terms.

Why there is no cross-channel CPL here
What this evidence does not establish

contextIntro: A Patna-based residential real estate client, with paid acquisition activity documented across two platforms.

The exports record what each campaign spent and delivered. They do not record a common start and end date for every campaign, so nothing here should be read as a claim that all {{metric:cc.campaigns|words}} campaigns were necessarily running concurrently.

metaTable.caption: Meta campaigns
metaTable.note: “Verified leads” means lead form submissions recorded by Meta. It does not mean independently qualified leads, and lead quality is not established by this evidence.

metaCommentary: The {{metric:cc.meta.campaigns|words}} Meta campaigns produced very different cost per lead — {{metric:cc.meta_1.cpl}} against {{metric:cc.meta_2.cpl}} — on the same platform, for the same client, in the same market.

That spread is the useful part. It says the difference sits in the campaign itself: the project, the offer, the audience or the creative. Those are testable. A blended Meta average across both would have hidden it.

googleTable.caption: Google Search campaigns
googleTable.note: Clicks are clicks. They are not leads, and they are not treated as leads anywhere on this page.

channelPanels.caveat: Google lead count is not verified from the available evidence.

content.comparisonCaution: These panels are deliberately not aligned into a single winner-versus-loser comparison. The two channels are being measured against different outcome definitions, and one of those definitions is not reliable in this dataset.
limitationBody: Google conversion reporting is not reliable in this dataset. The campaign exports show conversion rates that cannot be reconciled with recorded click volume — figures such as {{metric:cc.google.reported_conversion_rate_1}}, {{metric:cc.google.reported_conversion_rate_2}} and {{metric:cc.google.reported_conversion_rate_3}}.
That rules out a Google cost per lead. It also rules out the comparison a client most often asks for: which channel produced cheaper leads.

The honest answer is that the question cannot be answered from this evidence, and answering it anyway — by dividing Google spend by Google clicks and calling the result a lead cost — would be the single most misleading thing this case study could do.

limitationRules.reason: The conversion denominator is not trustworthy.

limitationRules.rule: The {{metric:cc.google.clicks}} clicks are never called {{metric:cc.google.clicks}} leads.
limitationRules.reason: A click is not a lead.
The two channels are not measured on the same outcome.

content.centralInsight: Cross-channel marketing only becomes comparable when both platforms report the same defined outcome.
content.limitationsIntro: The evidence here covers spend and platform-recorded activity across two channels. It does not establish:
limitations: Which channel produced better business outcomes
content.limitationsClosing: The exports also do not record a common start and end date for all {{metric:cc.campaigns|words}} campaigns, so this is a record of documented activity across two platforms rather than a like-for-like comparison of two channels running side by side.

takeaway.heading: The strongest cross-channel lesson is measurement comparability.
notComparable: Which channel produced better business outcomes
body: Spend, clicks, click-through rate, cost per click and campaign structure can all be compared across channels today. They are measured the same way on both platforms.

Meaningful acquisition comparison needs something else: the same trustworthy outcome definition on both sides. Until a lead means the same thing in Meta and in Google — and until both platforms record it dependably — a cross-channel budget decision is being made on a number that only one channel actually has.
That is fixable, and fixing it is usually worth more than any bid adjustment made in the meantime.
